pages.text: Home/Insights/ECOMMERCEECOMMERCEShopify vs WooCommerce vs Custom Ecommerce: How to ChooseCompare Shopify, WooCommerce and custom ecommerce by catalogue complexity, integrations, operating costs and the team running your store.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 20 October 2026On this pageWhat is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?How large and complex is your catalogue?Who will run the store every day?What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?What does total cost of ownership include?How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?Worked example: the requirement that decides the platformWhat to do nextWhat to considerShopify is hosted and managed for you, WooCommerce is a WordPress plugin you host yourself, and a custom store is software built around your own rules.The deciding factors are usually who runs the store day to day, how complex your catalogue is, and which systems must connect to it, not the feature list.Compare total cost of ownership, not the build quote: hosting, apps or plugins, maintenance, payment fees and developer time all recur.Choose custom or headless only when a specific, revenue-relevant journey cannot be done on a standard platform.Replatforming carries real SEO and data risk, so plan URL redirects, product data migration and a rollback path before you commit.Shopify vs WooCommerce comes down to who runs the store and how unusual your way of selling is. Shopify is a hosted platform that looks after the infrastructure for you. WooCommerce is a plugin for WordPress that you host and maintain yourself. A custom store is worth building only when a standard platform cannot support a journey that earns you money.The best choice is rarely the platform with the longest feature list. It is the one your team can run on an ordinary Tuesday without calling a developer, and that will still fit the business in two years. This guide gives you the criteria, a comparison table and a short process for deciding.What is the real difference between Shopify, WooCommerce and a custom store?The real difference is who carries responsibility. With Shopify, a vendor hosts the platform, runs the checkout infrastructure and ships core updates, and you configure the store, choose a theme and add apps. With WooCommerce, you or your agency choose hosting, update WordPress, the plugin and every extension, and take care of security and backups. With a custom store, you own all of it.That gives you a simple way to think about it. Shopify trades some flexibility for convenience. WooCommerce trades convenience for control over the code, the database and the content. Custom trades speed and low upkeep for the freedom to model your business exactly. None of the three is better in general. Each is better for a particular kind of team.How large and complex is your catalogue?Catalogue complexity matters more than catalogue size. A few thousand simple products with sizes and colours suit all three options. Trouble starts with unusual structures: made-to-order products with many dependent options, bundles with rules, B2B price lists per customer, rental or booking items, or products that need a configurator before they can be priced.Ask three questions. Can every product be described as a title, images, variants and a price? Do prices or availability depend on who is buying? Does a buyer need to configure the product before adding it to the basket? If the answers are yes, no and no, a hosted platform is usually the quickest route. If the second or third answer is yes, list exactly which rules you need and check whether a maintained app or plugin covers them before you consider custom work.Who will run the store every day?The person who edits products, processes orders and runs promotions should shape the decision. A marketing or operations lead who wants to launch a collection or a discount without developer help usually does well on Shopify, because the admin is built for merchants. A team that already publishes content on WordPress may find WooCommerce natural, because products, posts and landing pages live in one system.Custom admin tools can be excellent when they are designed around your exact workflow, but they only help if someone owns their evolution. Be honest about capacity. If nobody on the team can look after plugin updates, backups and hosting, a self-hosted store will slowly become a risk. If you want deep control and have a developer or agency on retainer, that same setup becomes an asset.Rule of thumbChoose the platform your least technical daily user can operate confidently. A powerful system that only one developer understands is a business risk, not an advantage.What about integrations, ERP and checkout customisation?Integrations decide more projects than design does. Write down every system the store must exchange data with: inventory or ERP, accounting, shipping, a CRM, a marketing tool, a returns process. For each one, note what moves in which direction and how often. Stock levels and orders are the usual pain points, because errors there cost money and customer trust.Shopify extends through apps and APIs, and its documentation describes checkout customisation through checkout UI extensions and Shopify Functions, which let you add interface elements and change business logic such as discounts, delivery options and payment rules. WooCommerce is extended with PHP hooks, filters, plugins and its REST API, so almost anything is possible but quality varies by plugin. A custom store lets you design the integration properly, at the price of building and maintaining it.If you run an ERP, ask early whether a maintained connector exists for your platform and who supports it when it breaks. Our integration solutions work often starts exactly here, with a clear data map between the store and the systems behind it.Project screenshot: Outcome summary workspace for Ecommerce Development.What does total cost of ownership include?Total cost of ownership is everything you pay to build, run and change the store over its life, not the build quote. Prices and plans change often, so check each vendor’s current pricing page rather than relying on an article. What you should do is list the cost categories so the three options are compared like for like.Platform or hosting: a subscription for a hosted platform, or hosting, a CDN and backups for a self-hosted one.Theme and design work, including future changes to templates.Apps or plugins, which often carry their own recurring fees, and the effort of keeping them compatible.Payment provider and transaction fees, which depend on your provider, region and plan.Developer time for integrations, bug fixes, updates and security patching.Staff time: how many hours a week your team spends working around limitations.Migration and exit costs if you outgrow the choice.Custom builds have the highest upfront cost and often the lowest per-feature friction later, but they also have the largest maintenance obligation. Hosted platforms look cheaper at the start and can accumulate app fees. Self-hosted WooCommerce can look cheapest on paper and then quietly cost developer hours. Model three years, not three months.How do performance, hosting and SEO control compare?Hosting responsibility is the clearest performance difference. On Shopify the platform handles servers and delivery, so your speed depends mostly on your theme, images and apps. On WooCommerce, speed also depends on your host, caching, database and plugin load, which gives you more control and more ways to go wrong. On a custom store, performance is whatever you engineer.For search, all three can rank well when built properly. WooCommerce sits on WordPress and offers fine control over URLs, templates and content. Shopify gives you editable titles, descriptions, redirects and sitemaps, though some URL patterns such as the products and collections prefixes are fixed. Custom stores give full control but require you to build SEO basics deliberately. Whichever route you take, plan for performance and search foundations, clean product data and structured markup from the start.Shopify vs WooCommerce vs custom: side-by-side comparisonUse this table to score each option against your own priorities. It describes general tendencies, not guarantees, so confirm the details for your own requirements before you decide. Give each row a weight from one to three based on how much it matters to your business, then see which column wins.Shopify, WooCommerce and custom ecommerce compared across the main decision criteriaCriterionShopifyWooCommerceCustom storeHosting modelHosted and managed by the vendorSelf-hosted on WordPress; you choose and manage hostingYou choose and manage everythingBest for catalogueStandard products and variantsContent-rich or moderately unusual cataloguesComplex configurators, rules and pricingDay-to-day adminMerchant-friendly, built for non-developersFamiliar if you already use WordPress; more upkeepWhatever is built; needs an ownerCheckout customisationThrough extensions and Shopify FunctionsHooks, filters and plugins; wide but uneven qualityFully designed to your rulesIntegrations and ERPApps and APIs; check connector supportPlugins and REST API; check maintenanceBuilt to your exact data flowsCost shape over timeSubscription plus apps and feesHosting, plugins and developer timeHighest upfront, ongoing engineeringPerformance responsibilityPlatform infrastructure; you manage theme and appsShared: host, caching, pluginsEntirely yoursSEO controlGood, with some fixed URL patternsVery high with WordPress toolingTotal, but built from scratchMigration risk laterModerate; data export and redirects neededModerate; you own the data and databaseHigher; custom data models are harder to moveWhen does headless or custom make sense, and what is the migration risk?Custom or headless commerce makes sense when a specific journey earns real revenue and a standard platform cannot support it. Headless means the shopping interface is built separately from the commerce engine and talks to it through an API. It can give you a faster, fully tailored front end, but it also means you maintain two layers, and many conveniences of a themed store become your responsibility.Good reasons include a product configurator, unusual B2B pricing, a subscription model with special rules, or an experience that spans content, community and commerce. Weak reasons include wanting a unique look alone, or assuming custom is automatically faster. Our custom ecommerce team tends to suggest proving the hardest journey with a small prototype first.Replatforming itself is risky whichever way you go. Products, customers, order history, reviews and URLs all have to move, and any URL that changes without a redirect can lose search visibility. Keep the old store running until the new one is verified, redirect every important URL, and agree a rollback path. Our search and visibility service includes a review of redirects, indexing and monitoring needs.Project screenshot: Outdoor equipment storefront.Worked example: the requirement that decides the platformImagine a merchant with ordinary products, a small editorial team and standard shipping. Its first comparison should establish whether a maintained Shopify or WooCommerce setup meets the workflow. A custom storefront is not automatically better because the design is distinctive.Now change one requirement: every order needs customer-specific pricing and approval by the buyer’s purchasing manager. Prototype that rule with the candidate platform before committing. Compare extension support, operating fees and failure handling with a custom workflow. These are hypothetical examples, not client outcomes.Can the required product be configured without a fragile collection of workarounds?Who reconciles stock and orders when a provider is unavailable?Which account owns the store, payment integration and source assets?Can the team test the hardest order before the full catalogue is migrated?Use the relevant scope guide to prepare the next conversation: Shopify development, WooCommerce development or custom ecommerce development. For synchronisation around an existing store, review ecommerce operations workflows.Checkout extension surfaces and plan eligibility can change. Verify the exact requirement using Shopify’s checkout development documentation, rather than assuming any requested checkout change is available on every plan.What to do nextTake an hour and do three things. List your ten most important products and any rules attached to them. List every system the store must connect to. Name the person who will run the store daily. With those three lists, most teams can already rule out one option.Then test the hardest journey, not the easiest. If you are leaning towards a hosted platform, our Shopify development work focuses on theme, catalogue and checkout. If WordPress is already part of your stack, see WooCommerce development. If neither fits, bring your list to a conversation and we will help you judge it honestly. You can contact us whenever you are ready.PROJECT CASE STUDIESSee the workflow in our project workExplore the screens and decisions behind related user journeys. Each case study explains its project context; the service choice for your own project follows your requirements.Skincare Ecommerce: DewSkin-preference filtering · Ingredient, texture and use-time comparison · Product-level add-to-bag actions.Read the project case study Inventory Management Software: StockroomReorder thresholds and recommendations · Purchase-order line-item review · Separate draft and approval actions.Read the project case study Discuss your projectCompare our ecommerce development services when you are ready to scope a store.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO & GEO: A Practical Website Improvement Plan ↗AI Automation for Business: 7 Workflows Worth Testing ↗How to Plan an MVP: Scope, Features & Validation ↗

pages.text: Home/Insights/AI & AUTOMATIONAI & AUTOMATIONAI Automation for Business: 7 Workflows Worth TestingExplore seven business automation workflows, how to rank them, where human review matters and how to measure a focused AI pilot.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 20 October 2026On this pageWhat makes a task worth automating with AI?Which seven workflows should you automate first?How do you rank the seven for your business?What should you not automate yet?How do you run a first pilot?Worked example: an enquiry-routing pilotWhat to do nextWhat to considerAI automation for business works best on tasks that repeat often, have a clear owner and can be checked quickly by a person.Start with workflows where a mistake is cheap to catch, such as drafting replies for approval, before touching anything that moves money or sends messages on its own.Every workflow needs a number you can measure before and after, such as minutes per task, first response time or share of drafts accepted without edits.Rank candidates by frequency, cost of error, data availability and ease, then pilot one workflow on real examples before building more.Some work should not be automated yet: unclear processes, high-stakes decisions and anything with no sample data to test against.AI automation for business means using AI models inside a defined workflow so that software handles the routine reading, sorting and drafting, while people handle the decisions. It is most useful on tasks that repeat often, follow a recognisable pattern and can be checked quickly.It is least useful when sold as a replacement for judgement. This guide gives seven workflows that usually make good first projects, a table to rank them for your own business, and a list of work that should wait. Each workflow is described the same way: what goes in, what the AI does, what a person still checks, and how to measure it.What makes a task worth automating with AI?A task is worth automating when it repeats often, has a clear owner, produces an output someone can check in seconds, and has examples you can test against. If you cannot describe the input, the expected output and what counts as a mistake, the task is not ready for AI yet.Four questions help. How often does it happen? What does a wrong result cost? Do you have past examples to test with? How many other systems must it connect to? A weekly task with expensive errors and no examples is a poor first project. A daily task with cheap errors and a shared inbox full of examples is a good one. Write down the current time per task before you start, because that is your baseline for every claim later.Which seven workflows should you automate first?These seven appear in most small and mid-sized businesses in some form. They are listed roughly from lowest risk to highest. In every case the AI prepares and a person approves, at least until you have evidence that the output is reliable enough to relax that rule.1. Enquiry triage and routingGoes in: emails, web form messages or chat enquiries.AI does: labels the type (sales, support, billing, spam), extracts key details such as company, product and urgency, and routes it to the right queue.Person checks: low-confidence items and a regular sample of routed ones.Measure: time from arrival to the right person seeing it, and the share of enquiries rerouted by hand.This is often the best first project because mistakes are visible and cheap to fix. A misrouted enquiry is slower, not catastrophic. Our business automation service typically starts here.2. Drafting replies for human approvalGoes in: a customer message plus your policies, past replies and product information.AI does: writes a draft reply in your tone and cites which policy or past answer it used.Person checks: every draft before it is sent, editing as needed.Measure: drafts accepted with no or light edits, minutes saved per reply, and complaints about tone or accuracy.Nothing is sent without approval, so the risk stays low while you learn how often the drafts are good. Edits are also useful data: patterns in what people change show you where the instructions or source documents need work.3. Document and invoice data extractionGoes in: invoices, purchase orders, forms, contracts or delivery notes, often as PDFs or photos.AI does: pulls out named fields such as supplier, date, line items and totals into a structured record.Person checks: fields that fail validation, such as totals that do not add up, and a sample of the rest.Measure: field-level accuracy against a hand-checked set, and time per document.Accuracy here can be measured field by field, which makes it one of the more honest workflows to evaluate. Add simple rules around the AI, for example rejecting a record where line items do not sum to the total.4. Meeting and call note summaries into the CRMGoes in: a call recording transcript or meeting notes, with permission from participants.AI does: summarises decisions, lists action items with owners, and proposes updates to CRM fields.Person checks: the summary and any CRM change before it is saved.Measure: minutes spent on admin after calls, and how many CRM records are complete a day later.The value is mostly consistency: notes get written and records get updated. Make sure you have consent to record and transcribe, and decide where transcripts are stored and for how long. A custom CRM can make the proposed updates easier to review.5. Internal knowledge searchGoes in: handbooks, policies, product sheets, past proposals and help articles.AI does: answers staff questions in plain language and shows the source passages it used.Person checks: the cited source when the answer matters, and owners review gaps the assistant reports.Measure: questions answered without asking a colleague, share of answers with a correct source, and searches that end in no result.This is the workflow behind most AI assistants. It only works as well as your documents, so budget time to clean them. Explore how a business AI assistant can use your own information with appropriate access controls.Project screenshot: Outcome summary workspace for AI & Automation.6. Lead qualification and follow-up prepGoes in: new leads from forms, ads or events, plus your definition of a good fit.AI does: summarises the company from public information, scores fit against your criteria, and drafts a first follow-up for the salesperson.Person checks: the score and the draft before anyone is contacted.Measure: time from lead to first contact, and whether high-scored leads convert better than low-scored ones.Track the last measure honestly. If scores do not predict outcomes, change the criteria rather than trust the number. See our sales and marketing automation work for how routing and follow-up preparation fit together.7. Report and dashboard commentaryGoes in: figures from your reports or business dashboards, plus last period for comparison.AI does: drafts a short written commentary on what changed and which numbers look unusual.Person checks: every figure quoted and every explanation offered, since the AI sees the numbers but not the reasons.Measure: time to produce the weekly report, and corrections made before it is shared.Keep the calculations in code or your reporting tool, not in the model. Let the AI describe numbers that are already computed, then have an analyst confirm the explanations.How do you rank the seven for your business?Score each candidate on four things: how often it happens, how costly a mistake is, whether you have example data, and how easy it is to connect. The table below shows a typical starting view. Treat the ratings as a prompt for discussion, because your business will differ.Typical starting ratings. Adjust to your own volumes and risks.WorkflowFrequencyCost of errorData availabilityEaseEnquiry triage and routingHighLowHigh (inbox history)MediumDraft replies for approvalHighLow (approved first)High (sent mail)MediumDocument and invoice extractionMedium to highMediumMediumMediumMeeting and call notes to CRMMediumLow to mediumMediumMediumInternal knowledge searchMediumLow to mediumDepends on document qualityMediumLead qualification and follow-up prepMediumMediumMediumMedium to hardReport and dashboard commentaryLow to medium (weekly)MediumHigh (the numbers exist)Easy to mediumPick the row where frequency is high, error cost is low and data exists. For many teams that is enquiry triage or drafted replies. If your biggest pain is somewhere else, such as invoices, start there, but add stricter validation because the cost of an error is higher.Rule of thumbIf you would be uncomfortable with a new hire doing the task on day one without review, the AI should not do it without review either. Begin with review, then relax it where your measurements justify it.What should you not automate yet?Leave a task alone when the process is unclear, a wrong answer is costly or irreversible, or you have no examples to test against. Automating a messy process produces a faster mess. These tasks are better left with people, or automated only up to a drafting step.Processes nobody can describe. Write the steps down first. If two people do it differently, agree one way before adding AI.Final decisions on money, contracts, hiring, health or legal matters. AI can prepare material, but a named person decides.Anything that sends messages or changes records with no review, until you have measured error rates on real examples.Tasks with no sample data. Without 30 to 50 real, representative cases you cannot tell whether the workflow works.Sensitive personal or confidential data you have not classified. Decide what may leave your systems before choosing tools.Rare, high-variety work such as one-off negotiations, where each case is different and the saving is small.How do you run a first pilot?Run one workflow, on real examples, with a person approving the output, and compare it with your baseline. A small pilot answers whether the workflow works for your data far more cheaply than a large build, and it shows where the real work is: usually in documents, permissions and integrations, not the model.Choose one workflow and write down its current time per task and error rate.Collect 30 to 50 real examples, including awkward ones, and agree what a good output looks like.Build the smallest version that connects to the real inbox, CRM or document store, with approval before anything is sent or saved.Run it alongside the current process for a set period and log accepted, edited and rejected outputs.Review the numbers, fix the biggest failure pattern, then decide whether to widen, change or stop.Project screenshot: Document-grounded support copilot.Plan for the unglamorous parts too: logging, access rights, a clear handoff when the AI is unsure, and someone who owns the workflow after launch. Demos show the idea; production needs these. If you are unsure whether you need a simple assistant, a workflow or something more autonomous, explore our AI and automation services first.Worked example: an enquiry-routing pilotConsider a hypothetical team that manually reads inbound project enquiries. A bounded pilot could validate required fields, suggest a service category and prepare a short handoff for staff approval. Straightforward routing rules should remain deterministic; AI is useful only where interpreting free text adds value.Collect a representative sample including duplicate messages, vague requests and unrelated enquiries. Compare suggestions with a named reviewer’s decisions. Record review time, incorrect assignments, edits and failed integrations. Define success before looking at the results; no particular time saving is assumed.Start without automatically sending customer replies.Keep the original enquiry available so a reviewer can inspect the source.Test missing information and provider timeouts, not only complete requests.Make retries safe so one enquiry does not create several CRM records.Different tasks need different scope: business automation handles routing and exceptions, AI assistants retrieve approved knowledge, and sales automation connects inbound lead context and reviewed follow-up. Use API integration services when data movement is the main requirement.What to do nextPick the workflow with the highest frequency, lowest cost of error and best example data, and measure how long it takes today. That one number is the start of a useful conversation about scope. You do not need a model chosen or a vendor shortlisted to do this.If you would like help ranking your own candidates or scoping a pilot, tell us which task is eating the most time through our contact page. We work in milestones with regular demos and agree what success looks like before building. Cost and timing depend on scope, so we talk them through with you rather than quote a number here.PROJECT CASE STUDIESSee the workflow in our project workExplore the screens and decisions behind related user journeys. Each case study explains its project context; the service choice for your own project follows your requirements.AI Customer Support Workspace: NexaOriginal conversation beside the draft · Visible source-record context · Explicit reply editing and approval.Read the project case study Lead Qualification & Routing: IntakeStructured project enquiry context · Separate qualification checks · Owner, team and next-action routing.Read the project case study Discuss your projectExplore business workflow automation to scope a reviewed pilot.CONTINUE READINGAnother useful perspective.SEO, AEO & GEO: A Practical Website Improvement Plan ↗Shopify vs WooCommerce vs Custom Ecommerce: How to Choose ↗How to Plan an MVP: Scope, Features & Validation ↗

pages.text: Home/Insights/PRODUCT ENGINEERINGPRODUCT ENGINEERINGHow to Plan an MVP: Scope, Features & ValidationPlan a software MVP around one customer journey. Compare build options, prioritise features, set milestones and validate assumptions with real users.By Cubusify Editorial · Updated 20 October 2026On this pageWhat is a minimum viable product, and what is it not?How do you choose one customer, one problem and one journey?Which assumption should you test first?How do you scope MVP features with must, should and could?Should you build, buy or use no-code for the first test?How do you set milestones and success metrics before building?How can AI help plan an MVP without replacing user conversations?When is an MVP the wrong tool?Worked example: a booking MVP scope briefWhat to do nextWhat to considerAn MVP is a learning tool: it exists to test your riskiest assumption with real users, not to ship a cheaper copy of the whole product.Scope around one customer, one problem and one complete journey that a user can start, finish and understand.Sort every feature into must, should or could, and cut anything you could do by hand for your first ten users.Define milestones as working outcomes and agree success metrics before building, so the result is a decision rather than an opinion.AI can speed up prototyping and research, but it cannot replace conversations with real customers.MVP development is the practice of building the smallest working version of a product that can test your riskiest assumption with real users. A minimum viable product is not a rough demo and not a thinned-out copy of your full vision. It is a complete but narrow first version: one customer, one problem and one journey that works from start to finish.To plan an MVP, name the customer and the problem, list your assumptions and pick the riskiest, sort features into must, should and could, and cut hard. Then define milestones as working outcomes and agree your success metrics before anyone writes code. The sections below take each step in turn, including when an MVP is the wrong tool.What is a minimum viable product, and what is it not?A minimum viable product is the smallest version of a product that delivers real value to a real user and teaches you something you could not learn by thinking. The word "minimum" limits the scope. The word "viable" sets the bar: someone must be able to complete a task and get a result they care about. Unlike a prototype, which may only show an idea, an MVP has to work for a user, even if it is narrow, manual in places and plain to look at.The most common mistake is treating the MVP as version one of the full product, with every feature made thinner. That gives you a wide, shallow build that tests nothing. A better frame is a question. For example, "will clinic managers stop using a paper diary if booking takes two taps?" is a question an MVP can answer. "Will people like our platform?" is not.How do you choose one customer, one problem and one journey?Choose the customer who feels the problem most often and already works around it, whether with a spreadsheet, a stack of messages or a paid tool they dislike. Narrow beats broad. A product for "small businesses" cannot be tested, because their needs differ too much. A product for one type of team with one painful weekly task can be. The workaround you can see today is evidence that the problem is real.Then write the journey as one sentence: "A customer can complete one task and see the result without help." If the sentence needs three "and" clauses, it is really three journeys. Pick the one that, if it worked, would make the customer say they would switch or pay. Everything else waits.Who exactly is the first user, and how will you reach ten of them?What do they do today instead, and what does it cost them in time or errors?What is the single action that proves they got value?What must be true before they can start, such as data, access or an account?One-sentence ruleIf you cannot describe the journey in one sentence, or you cannot name ten real people who could try it, the scope is still too wide or the customer too vague. Fix that before you plan any features.Project screenshot: Outcome summary workspace for Product Engineering.Which assumption should you test first?Test the assumption that would end the project if it were wrong and for which you have the least evidence. Every product rests on assumptions about whether people want it (desirability), whether you can build it (feasibility) and whether the business works (viability). Assumption mapping makes them visible, so your first weeks go to the one that matters most rather than the one that is easiest to build.List every assumption behind your idea, one per line, such as "managers will enter the data themselves" or "customers will pay monthly".Score each one for the damage if it is wrong and for how little evidence you have today.Circle the ones that score high on both. These are your riskiest assumptions.Pick one and design the smallest test that could prove it wrong.Decide in advance what result would make you continue, change direction or stop.Often the riskiest assumption is not technical. It is "will they change their habit?" or "will they give us access to their data?" Test those with a conversation or a clickable mock-up first, and save engineering for assumptions only working software can test.How do you scope MVP features with must, should and could?Sort every candidate feature by one test: does the core journey fail without it? If yes, it is a must. If the journey works but is clumsier, it is a should. If it is merely nice to have, it is a could. Be strict: a real MVP scope has a short list of musts and a long list of coulds you will not touch.A scoping table for a hypothetical appointment-booking MVPBucketTest to applyExample featuresDecisionMustThe journey fails without itChoose a time slot, confirm the booking, see the confirmationBuild nowShouldThe journey works but is clumsier without itEmail reminder, reschedule linkBuild only if time remains after the mustsCouldNice to have, and no user has asked for it yetCalendar sync, loyalty points, custom themesLeave out and note in a backlogNot nowA real need, but risky or costly for a first testOnline payments, multiple locations, role permissionsReplace with a manual step or deferCutting is where most MVPs are won or lost. Common things to remove from a first version include admin panels (use a database view or spreadsheet instead), user roles and permissions (start with one role), settings pages, multiple payment methods, polished onboarding, reporting suites and integrations with tools your first users do not rely on. Each can be replaced by a manual step.Do it by hand firstIf a person can do a task for your first ten customers, do it by hand and learn from doing it. Automate it only once you know it matters and you understand how it really works.Should you build, buy or use no-code for the first test?Use the cheapest tool that can still answer your question. For a first test that may be a configured SaaS product, a no-code builder or a form connected to a spreadsheet. Custom code makes sense when the journey itself is the product, when a no-code tool cannot deliver the experience users need, or when the demand is already proven and you want to build it properly.Choosing a route for the first testRouteBest whenWatch out forBuild customThe experience or logic is the product, or you need control over data and performanceHighest upfront effort, and it is easy to build more than the test needsBuy or configure SaaSA standard tool already covers most of the journeyPer-user costs and limits on how far you can change itNo-code or low-codeYou need a working interface quickly to test demandLimits on scale, performance and data portability; a rebuild may followConcierge or manualYou are unsure the customer wants the outcome at allDoes not scale and does not test technical feasibilityNone of these choices is permanent. Many good products began as a no-code test and were rebuilt once demand was proven. If you are weighing longer-term tooling rather than a quick test, our custom software team can help assess the criteria.Project screenshot: Customer feedback discovery board.Can you fake the product first? The concierge and Wizard of Oz shortcutYes, and it is often the fastest route to learning. In a concierge MVP you deliver the outcome by hand and the customer knows it: you are the product. In a Wizard of Oz MVP the customer sees a working interface while people do the work behind it. Both test whether the outcome is wanted before you pay to automate it.These shortcuts have limits. They do not prove the software can be built, they do not scale, and they can hide how much manual effort the real product will need. Be honest with users about how their data is handled. AI can play part of the wizard, for example by drafting replies, but a person should check the output before a customer relies on it.How do you set milestones and success metrics before building?Define milestones as working outcomes a person can try, not as lists of screens. "The login and dashboard pages are done" tells you little. "A new user can complete the booking journey on a phone and the clinic sees it" tells you the product works. Each milestone ends with a demo, so you can see progress, correct course early and stop if the evidence says so.A user can start and finish the core journey on a test account.The first real users can complete it without help from the team.The person on the other side, such as the admin or manager, can see and act on the result.Events are recorded so you can see where people drop out.A review compares what happened with the success metric you agreed.Set success metrics before you build, while you are still neutral. Choose one primary metric tied to the journey, such as the share of started journeys that finish or the number of users who return unprompted. Write down the threshold that counts as success and what you will do if you miss it. Without this, every result can be explained away.Instrumentation is how you get the data. At a minimum, record when a user starts the journey, each step they complete, where they leave and when they finish. Pair those numbers with short conversations, because analytics show what happened and people tell you why. Add tracking in the first milestone. A review of the journey with user experience design before you build often removes a whole round of rework. This is also how we work at Cubusify under Results as a Service: define the goal, deliver in milestones with demos and measure what changes.How can AI help plan an MVP without replacing user conversations?AI is useful for speed during planning and weak at the thing that matters most: telling you what real customers want. Use it to draft, summarise and prototype. Do not use it to decide. A language model can produce confident, plausible answers about customers who do not exist, and it will not warn you when it is wrong.Summarise and tag interview notes or transcripts, once participants have agreed and sensitive details are removed, then check the themes against the originals.Draft user stories, acceptance criteria and test cases that your team reviews and edits.Generate clickable prototypes and sample data so you can put something in front of users sooner.Scan public competitor material and documentation for questions worth asking, treating the output as leads to verify rather than facts.What AI cannot do is replace talking to ten real people. Synthetic personas and AI-generated "customer feedback" are not evidence. Treat AI as a way to prepare better conversations and to build the test faster, never as the test itself.When is an MVP the wrong tool?An MVP is the wrong tool when the question is already answered or when "minimum" is not acceptable. If you are automating a well-understood internal process, the requirements are known and you should build the full solution in milestones. If the product handles payments, health records or other regulated data, security and compliance cannot be trimmed to fit a first test. And if you cannot reach any real users, building will not fix that. Sometimes the cheaper test is no software at all: a landing page or a manual pilot. If one of those can answer your riskiest assumption, do that first.Worked example: a booking MVP scope briefImagine an appointment-based business testing whether customers will request a slot online instead of calling. The first release could show the service, collect a preferred time, let staff accept or decline, and show the resulting status. It should not imply instant confirmation if staff still control availability.A staff-reviewed request flow can test interest before adding automatic scheduling, payments and several locations. The brief should still include permissions, duplicate submissions and a recovery path if confirmation fails. These are essential parts of the chosen task, not optional polish.Illustrative one-page MVP brief — no client result impliedDecisionExampleCustomerPeople booking one defined appointment service.AssumptionThey will complete an online request without a staff call.Core journeyChoose a service, request a time and understand the accepted or declined status.Out of scope initiallyPayments, loyalty programmes and multi-location scheduling.EvaluationAgree a completion threshold before the pilot and pair usage records with short customer conversations.Bring that brief to an MVP development discussion. If the main uncertainty is usability, begin with UX research and prototyping. If the product is already running and needs ongoing feature delivery, SaaS engineering is a different engagement.What to do nextThis week, write your one-sentence journey, list your assumptions and circle the riskiest. Then sort your feature list into must, should and could, and challenge every must. Bring that page, plus a sketch or your current spreadsheet, to a conversation. Concrete examples make scope easier to agree.If you would like a second pair of eyes, our MVP development work starts with exactly this: discovery, scope and a milestone plan. Cost and timeline depend on the scope, so the sensible first step is a short conversation.
